en: Sutta Nipāta 4.14 Tuvaṭakasutta “I ask you, O Kinsman of the Sun:”
O Great Seer, having seen what does a bhikkhu attain discernment and the state of peace, and how,
by not clinging to anything in the world, does he become extinguished?
“The root of the proliferation of conceptualization—
‘I am the thinker’— one should completely cut off all of this,” said the Blessed One.
Whatever craving there is within oneself,
one should always train with mindfulness for its removal;
whatever phenomenon one may fully understand...
Whether internally or even externally,
one should not take strength from that;
for that is not said by the virtuous to be true peace.
Touched by various forms, one should not think, "I am better than that," or "I am inferior," or even "I am equal."
A bhikkhu should not stand constructing a self-concept;
he should find peace within himself alone,
for he would not find peace from anything else.
For one who is inwardly stilled,
there is no self, so how could there be a "non-self"?
Like the middle of the ocean, [there is only the cessation of becoming].
As a wave arises and subsides,
so too, being thus established,
a bhikkhu who is unshakable should not give rise to arrogance toward anything at all.
“The one with the open eye has proclaimed the Dhamma witnessed by himself, which removes all dangers;
tell us, O Blessed One, the path.”
The Pātimokkha or even meditative concentration.
One who is not restless with the eyes should close the ear to village talk;
One should not crave flavors,
nor should one claim anything in the world as "mine.
When one is touched by contact—
A bhikkhu should not lament for anything anywhere;
he should not yearn for existence, nor should he tremble at fears.
Having obtained food, drinks,
hard foods, and even clothing,
one should not make a store.
One should not despair when failing to obtain those things.
A meditator should not be fickle with his feet;
he should abstain from remorse and not be negligent.
Then, in dwellings and lodgings that are free from noise, a bhikkhu should live;
he should not indulge in excessive sleep.
One should devote oneself to wakefulness with ardor;
one should abandon sloth, deceit, laughter, play,
sexual intercourse, and adornment.
One should not practice the science of portents, dream interpretation,
or physiognomy, nor should one engage in astrology,
the analysis of animal cries, or the induction of pregnancy.
My disciple should not practice medicine;
he should not be shaken by blame,
nor should the bhikkhu be elated when praised.
One should cast away greed along with stinginess, anger, and slander;
one should not engage in buying and selling.
A bhikkhu should not utter reproach against anyone anywhere;
he should not become attached to a village,
nor should he flatter people out of a desire for gain.
A bhikkhu should not be boastful,
nor should he utter speech that is purposeless;
he should not practice impudence.
How should one not engage in contentious talk?
One should not be led into falsehood,
and being clearly comprehending, one should not act with deceit.
Then, by means of life, wisdom,
or virtue and observances, one should not despise another.
Having heard much speech that is offensive, [one should remain composed].
Whether toward ascetics or ordinary people,
one should not respond with harshness,
for the virtuous do not retaliate.
Having understood this Dhamma,
a bhikkhu should always train himself, investigating with constant mindfulness;
knowing that "peace" is Nibbāna.
One should not be negligent regarding the teaching of Gotama.
For he is the conqueror who is unconquered,
the seer of the Dhamma through his own realization, which is timeless.
Therefore, indeed, in the teaching of that Blessed One,
one should always train diligently while paying homage.
Thus ends the fourteenth sutta, the Tuvaṭaka Sutta.
